utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The proceedings will continue under Rule 15 bis, paragraph A, as Judge Williams is not with us. Examination-in-chief continues, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Pantelic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic. Yesterday, just before we adjourned, I asked you several questions with respect to the members of the Crisis Staff, and you started giving us some explanations. But having looked at the lists I have here, I'd like to go back to that topic with a few more questions. First of all, tell us this, please: Mr. Miroslav Tadic, do you know when he became a member of the Crisis Staff and on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Miroslav Tadic became a member of the Crisis Staff when he became the head of civil defence or civilian protection. That was after the Crisis Staff had been established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was probably sometime in April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was sometime in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question with respect to this line of questioning: Mr. Fadil Topcagic, as you yourself said, was also a member of the Crisis Staff in that time frame. Did he have the right to vote? Did he have a vote within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fadil Topcagic was mentioned as being a member of the Crisis Staff, but he hardly ever took part in the work of the Crisis Staff, actually. And I interpret this as the fact that many people who were there actually didn't have any assignments, didn't have any field that was assigned to them. And Fadil Topcagic did not take part in fact work of the Crisis Staff, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But formally he did have a vote. He carried a vote, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question with respect to Mr. Savo Popovic and party membership. You said he was a member of the SDP. However, I should like to ask you whether you would like to add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was a member of the League of Communists. Now, whether in the meantime he joined the SDP, moved over to the SDP that had just been set up, quite possibly. But what I do know for certain is that he was not at any of the party lists for the elections on the 18th of November, 1990, so that possibly he was not actually a member of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Now tell me, please, in those first few days, what was your actual work? What did your work in the Crisis Staff entail? Could you give us an outline of your activities.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me try and recollect what I did during that period of time. I knew that there was general chaos and the situation was highly unsettled and muddled, and so somebody who like myself had a special assignment - mine was in the sector of information - had to do many other things as well. In fact, everybody had to do everything. For example, if there was a power cut anywhere, then we'd have to see to that. If a member of the Crisis Staff was free at that particular time, he would be assigned to see what he could do about that, to put the matter right. Or another example: If there was a shortage of water or a food shortage, one of the Crisis Staff might be called upon to intervene and see what could be done. So during that time frame, the Crisis Staff in fact coordinated activities of these kind in order to try and put a bit of order into the general chaos and to control it in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in those first few days, or rather, in that first week after mid-April 1992 technically speaking what did the -- what were the meetings like? Where was the seat of the Crisis Staff? Where did you have your meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first few days, our headquarters was in the social company that I already mentioned, PIK, the factory farm, the agricultural and industrial combine, and also in another socially-owned enterprise called Uniglas. And those two enterprises were located next to each other. They were buildings side by side, so both those buildings were used as headquarters for the Crisis Staff, depending on where we could get the job done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, but could we have a map. Could we have the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Exhibit D27/3, please. I do apologise. We're not receiving -- Your Honour, we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have a problem with the display. Maybe now it will be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: With what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With the ELMO transmission on our displays. We don't have a -- now it's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take up that metal pointer. I think it's right by the microphone. Can you see it, the metal pointer, witness? There it is in front of you. And now show us where the PIK company was. Show us on the map, please, the PIK factory farm.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see it on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you look at the paper. Don't look at the screen. Look at the paper in front of you and point with your pointer the location of the PIK company.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take it nice and slowly. Let's see the PIK company first.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, how long was the Crisis Staff's headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one or two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where did it move to then?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Uniglas building for another day or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And later on, where was the headquarters of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the power plant -- heating plant, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point that out to us.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the heating -- heating plant near the stadium or in that district?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Show us, please. Could you show us once again, point it out once again for us, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the steel and Buducnost company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness identified on the Exhibit D97/3 positions of the three premises of Crisis Staff, PIK, and then Uniglas company, and then heating plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Here it says "on Exhibit D97/3." It was actually D27/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The correct ID number is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Exhibit number is D27/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would like to thank to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Tell me, please, Mr. Simic: The activities of the Crisis Staff, what did they consist of? Or rather, tell us what the meetings looked like. Was there an agenda? Who drew up the proposals? What topics were discussed by the Crisis Staff in that first period, in the first few weeks of April? Is that kind of thing. Tell us something about that, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that initial period, and especially in the first couple of days, there was a lot to do in the field on the ground, if I can put it that way, so we didn't actually have time to hold meetings and Crisis Staff sessions. And as the Samac municipality was cut -- or rather, as all forms of communication in Samac were cut, the telephone lines were down, the communications, the goods and services, it was in a closed session, so it was within this area that chaos reigned. It was all one big disorder, like an ant hill, everybody rushing around and everybody doing all sorts of work. And I'm going to try and point out the three dominant areas. We had to focus on food for the people, food supplies for the population, because the companies had stopped working, production had ceased, and we had to take care of the ill and the wounded, the people who had been injured, and there were many problems that had to be solved, problems which you don't think about in peacetime but in extraordinary situations of this kind, they appear to be problems and you have to deal with them. What we also had to do was to organise production, so that little by little we could bring the companies back to operational order. So the Crisis Staff discussed matters of that kind. And from time to time it would take part in these activities, or rather, individual members of the Crisis Staff did. The Crisis Staff also set up a professional service of its own, and this was headed by Mr. Mitar Mitrovic. He was a lawyer by profession. And there was an information service as well. As to the other members, I don't know what each of them -- what each of their assignments were and what they actually did, but I do know that Mr. Popovic, for example, was in charge of coordinating the work of the Crisis Staff with the local communities and some physical geographical aspects had to be looked into, which means that he had to coordinate with some 20 villages. These villages did not have any modern means of communication amongst themselves, so he had to establish something like that. They didn't have any telephone links or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself, you personally, what was your assignment? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was the following: First of all, I helped get the radio station back into operation, and I did my best to organise information activity, which meant first of all the Samac radio station. At that time Samac didn't have a newspaper of its own, so I stepped in. There was -- the newspaper media did not exist. I also had to establish contact with the rest of the media, those who were interested in broadcasting information, and we would give them the information, which was then broadcast and published in Yugoslavia, the Yugoslavia media. I was also in charge of welcoming a television crew and journalists, to help them in those first contacts in Samac, to help them find their way more easily and to be able to do their job as journalists more easily. And let me say that we had a lot of problems with the radio station, because one day after the establishment of the Crisis Staff, I talked to the editor-in-chief of Samac Radio. His name was Mr. Vaso Antic. And he told me that the radio station was unable to function because the building itself in which the transmitter was located - and it is right next door to the secondary school building which had been set fire to -- to the elementary school building - and that the transmitter had also been damaged and couldn't be used. The Samac radio station, let me say, at that time had three frequencies. It was broadcast over three frequencies; that is to say, before the war. One was medium, the medium wave frequency, and two UKT frequencies, short wave. However, it was only able to broadcast on the medium wave frequency, and it had a transmitter to the power of 100 watts, which had been damaged in a fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said UKT. Could you describe what you mean by UKT.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UKT, ultra short waves and medium waves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the radio station was not operational. However, the editor-in-chief who had already established his own mini journalistic team, said that he could do something about it to make the station operational, at least to perform work in a modest framework. They had some equipment which had been decommissioned, and within that equipment they found a transmitter, UKT transmitter, which had very low power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we move fairly fast. We don't need the details. Simply go ahead. Was it repaired? Did it operate?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Instead of all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Simic. Just tell us what happened in the end. Were you able to repair it, fix it, and to have the staff of journalists start working?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That small transmitter was repaired. However, it worked only for one day and only one hour at that, and then afterward it broke down again. I was told that there was some kind of problem with it overheating and that as a result of that, something in the equipment had been damaged, so that for the next 10 to 15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. After it broke down after one day for an hour, was it repaired again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long did it operate after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, the transmitter worked all the way up until mid-1992, when a new one a different, a more powerful transmitter, was procured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as to the electric power, can you tell us how did that electric power supply impact the operation of the radio station.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had a direct impact because we had constant power outages, so that presented an additional problem. So during those first month and a half to two, the radio station wasn't really very useful as a media outlet. As a result of that, we tried to overcome that problem, and a bulletin was established, a written paper, leaflet, that informed about the events on the ground. But since this bulletin had a circulation of some 30 to 50 copies in total, the information of public continued to be a problem. I have to add though that some other newspapers would occasionally print or publish stories from our area. There were even some television programmes that dealt with this as well. I think that in late May, early June we in our information service produced two programmes, or rather, we taped footage to be used in two television programmes that were later to be broadcast by the Radio Television Serbia. I can tell you what topics they dealt with. The first one had to do with the shelling of Samac. The second one dealt with the participation of the Croatian army in operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to comment on a document that presents part of this court's records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can now take a look at this document on the ELMO. You can see it in its entirety. On the ELMO. Tell me, please, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It was passed on the same day when the Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon reading the preamble of this document, one can see that paramilitary formations are mentioned in it and then terror against innocent population and so on. Can you give me more details about the circumstances under which this document was drafted. What did it refer to?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The starting point for the document was that the situation in which we found ourselves was not regular. It was abnormal. Therefore, this decision on introducing state of emergency was passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us please go back to my question. Please take a look at the preamble, the introduction part of this document. You can see it on the ELMO. You can read it out for yourself, just to remind yourself.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the paramilitary formations which were organised by the Party of Democratic Action and the Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me something else, please. This mentions the incursion of the paramilitary formations. From which territory did they come from?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had in mind members of the Croatian army and the incursion of them from that area. That area across the Sava River was in the Republic of Croatia. And they supported this incursion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you personally learn about this situation, about this incursion?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about this during those days when they arrived, when these documents reached the Crisis Staff, these documents that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Posavina region, what was the situation like, say in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he keeps on using the word "they." He's talking about these documents. Is he talking about this particular document? He learned about this when he received this particular document? It's not clear what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, you mentioned the information about the incursion of these troops, and then you mentioned some documents. What did you have in mind? Let's take it step by step. You as a member of the Crisis Staff on the 19th passed this decision, I mean, the Crisis Staff as an institution did. And this decision was passed based on something. We would like to know now what was the basis for drafting this decision and especially this introductory part of it, the preamble. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what you knew at the time about certain facts, if you knew about them. And if you didn't, let us continue with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can sit, because I will discuss this document with some more questions, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so you know what we're interested in. This document was passed. It had an introductory part, the preamble. Give us some more details regarding it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting itself, the members of the Crisis Staff learnt the details about what had been prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they learn it from?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They learned it from certain services which monitored this and from the military and the police services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular individual involved in this? Did somebody come and report about this, or was there a written report that had arrived?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was announced in the introductory speech, and there had been people there who had been informed. I can't really remember now in that chaotic situation who was the one who came with those papers, but they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they say? What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that from the Republic of Croatia -- in the Republic of Croatia there had been some forces ready to make an incursion into Samac. Then we were told that in the territory of Odzak municipality there were some forces there ready to attack from the flank and that in Samac itself there had been armed formations called the Green Berets, members of the Croatian Defence Forces, HOS, and members of the HVO. And it wasn't difficult to find confirmation for that because in the PIK itself, on that first day when we came in to have our session there, there were some 30 people that had been found there wearing ZNG uniforms [As interpreted]. This was no surprise, in view of the fact that the director of that company was Mr. Bozanovic, who had used that enterprise as a logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a matter of clarification of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of the transcript. Here on page 13, line 17, it says that there were some 30 people that had been found there wearing ZNG uniforms. Actually, the witness was just talking about finding uniform, not about capturing some 30 men with ZNG uniforms. He said that they found uniforms, not people wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: With the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard what the problem is with the transcript. You told us what was found then, in the PIK premises.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniforms of the ZNG had been found, that is, the uniforms that had been worn by the regular Croatian troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their colours? Can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were multicoloured uniforms, green-grey colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you mentioned Mr. Bozanovic, who was the director of that enterprise, can you tell us his full name and what was his ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Marko Bozanovic, and he's an ethnic Croat. He was a commander of the newly created Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell me this: As we are analysing this document, we can see in item 6 of this decision something that I would like to ask you about now. How long did the state of emergency exist for?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you a theoretical answer to that. I cannot describe what is a state of emergency and what is a regular state. As far as I'm concerned, the state of emergency continues all the way up until the regular life is re-established, and that did not happen in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first session of the municipal assembly held in 1992? Not counting the founding assembly in February that we had mentioned -- or rather, let me ask you this: Had it been held, was it in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the first session of the municipal assembly in Samac was held on the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, how long did the Crisis Staff exist under that name?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff functioned under that name until July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that what body took over and functioned then, in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that there was the War Presidency, which had been established pursuant to some decree which existed and which had been presented to us by the Secretary of the municipal assembly, Mr. Mitar Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The War Presidency, was it another body, or rather, the second body in line in respect of the Crisis Staff, with respect to the number of members, et cetera, or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the number-two body, because the documents prescribed who could become a member of the War Presidency, those who were eligible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decree on the introduction of a state of emergency and point 7 in the contents of this document, was it made public or was it just restricted to the Crisis Staff? And if the population did know about it, how was it made public?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was never made public. It was never published in any form of information media. And the citizens were able to learn about it because there would be a copy which was paraphrased and sent out by way of a piece of information, and it was disseminated in the form of a leaflet or pamphlet. And one of the leaflets would be sent to the local commune, which informed people about what was going on. But many of the citizens never received this information, so point 7 of this document is a sort of -- more of a formal piece of rather information rather than actual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the previous document while we're waiting for this next one to be found, what kind of typewriter was used, what kind of letters? What kind of technical equipment did the Crisis Staff have?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Crisis Staff had a typewriter with the Cyrillic script. And the decisions it made were typed out on this typewriter in the Cyrillic script, and it still exists.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating the number of the exhibit. It's not on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's P79, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take a look at this document, please. It's on your right-hand side. What can you tell us about that document, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proclamation was primarily intended for the use of the media. And there was a follow-up to it, or rather, the media and agencies studied it and it was disseminated. I'm not sure whether it was actually broadcast over our own radio station, because on the day that the programme was interrupted because there was breakdown in the equipment -- actually, what I'm saying is I don't know if that proclamation was ever broadcast. But if it was, then it appeared in that form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? It's written in the Latin script, typewritten, again. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when this proclamation was typed out and compiled, the Crisis Staff and its service was in -- either in the PIK company building or the Uniglas company building, so the person who typed this out probably used one of the typewriters they found in one of the two firms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And explain this to me, please: The header in the top left-hand corner, which is handwritten, why was that written up in hand? Do you happen to know? I'm especially interested in the date, which is the 17th of April. Was this document in fact compiled on the 17th of April, as it says, or do you know something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document was drafted on the 19th of April. It came into being on the 19th of April. I don't know why anybody made this handwritten addition. I can only assume that this was written in subsequently. And in the workers' booklets, for example, that people had, this date, the 17th, would be written in, so that workers would have no interruption in their work, in their work booklets. So I can only assume that that was why this date was written in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, what was the basis of the information contained in paragraph 1 of this document? Take a look at the right-hand side. It's not a very legible copy, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like the previous decision and document we saw. The same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this: I can see a stamp here, and there was a stamp on the previous document as well. Why didn't it say "Crisis Staff" on the stamp? How do you explain what it says on the stamp here, the wording on the stamp? And I think it says "The Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac," I think -- "Pelagicevo." I think that's what it says. What do you know about that and what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the stamp is concerned, there was a separate department in charge of stamps. I can't really give you any more information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could we have now, please, Exhibit P3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take a look at this document. Leaf through it. Take it in your hands, put it in front of you, and have a perusal of it. Look at the title of the document, the date, and all the rest. Have you had a chance to look through it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this document discussed by anybody before 1992, in 1992, or later on? Did you ever hear anybody mention a document with this heading, with this title?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I've never heard of the existence of anything like this, and I don't know that anybody discussed this particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Usher. We can take this document, please. Now I would like to discuss a document, P73, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, do you remember this document by any chance?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we continue and before I answer your question, can I say the following: I would like to establish my position and say that the Crisis Staff never discussed things by being given a written document and then going on to discuss the written document and adopt it or not adopt it. The procedure was different. It made its decisions in the following way: A topic would be placed on the agenda. The Crisis Staff would discuss it. And then its professional service would sit down to write the document required. So I remember that on the agenda of one of the Crisis Staff meetings we did discuss this issue. This topic was on the agenda, but the form that the decision took and how it was written, as we can see it here, was something that was compiled later on. So this isn't something I can comment on in that way. But I do remember that a decision of this kind did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the actual subject under discussion. Now, could you take a look at the signature. Whose signature is that? Is it Dr. Blagoje Simic's signature, if you happen to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise his signature at all if you saw it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, Exhibit P74. And this one may rest for a second just, to make a small comparison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you place one document next to the other and tell me whether you recognise the signature on this new document to your left, on your left. I know you're not an expert in handwriting, but perhaps you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were in that body, a member of the body for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He indicated he wasn't familiar with the signature, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know you're not an expert, but at first glance, are they the same signatures?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He told you he can't recognise the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So why are you pressing him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was not a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me this: Do you remember the order of the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Usher. Yes. It's P74.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in point 1. What comment can you make -- how can you comment point 1 of this order? What was the purpose of it, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can remember what this referred to, the situation. Let me explain it in this way: It was customary -- I have to give you a longer answer in order to explain what I mean. In the former system, the army was considered to be a popular army, an army of the people, and we saw the army being depicted in Partisan films and things of that kind. And customary for the people to organise luncheons for the army, and this was what they did in this war too. The soldiers were also the sons of farmers, people from the grass roots, the salt of the earth. And in order to help the army, the people organised lunches for the soldiers. I'm not sure that I have explained this very well, but I did my best in the short space of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's a term used here "special battalion." What can you tell us about this special battalion? Who was it? Who made up the special battalion? Who was the commander? How many members did it have? Things like that. Can you tell us anything about that, and the purpose of the battalion itself.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the battalion and this military issue, I can't really tell you a great deal, but what I do know is the following: The special battalion consisted of young men who at that time did not wish to be mere static soldiers, that is to say, to be deployed up at the front line and just stand there. They wanted to take part in offensives, in offensive operations. And then once they had completed this military action, they wanted to have a longer spell to rest. Otherwise, they were mostly young people from Samac and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many made up the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the volunteers who had come in from Serbia? When did you hear about volunteers, if you ever heard about them?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were volunteers in the army, but the -- there was very scant information about them, hardly any at all. All I do know is that one of them would sow the seeds of fear, and he was known as Lugar [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other name comes to mind when you mention the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a man called Crni.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Meaning "black." Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something wrong with the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- that I noticed. The witness said, when speaking about Lugar, he was the one who would sow the seed of fear among Serb population. This is what we heard, and I don't see this in the transcript. It's on page 22, line 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic can deal with that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about Lugar, what were you trying to say? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the following: I didn't hear anything about other volunteers. I have no information about them. However, I did hear things about this one, and that was within the context that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat that context, because it wasn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sowed fear among the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way? What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he had physically abused soldiers, residents, and so on that, he got drunk frequently, that he was very aggressive. In one word, that he was a man who terrorised the people around him, terrorised his environment. I even think, now that I recollect this - I don't know if it was in late May or early June, but one of the people in the Crisis Staff security told me that on one occasion Lugar came to the Crisis Staff premises and this man from the Crisis Staff security told me that Lugar had been drunk. The security did not dare stop him. However, this man from the security followed him from one room into another. Lugar was looking to find somebody. And then he turned around and asked him, "What were you doing there?" And then the man from the security said, "Well, I'm just here doing my job." And then Lugar cursed him and told him that it would be better for him to go to the front line, and then he turned one more time and said, "Where is that fat Blagoje?" And by saying "fat," he wanted to insult and humiliate the president of the Crisis Staff, and he also wanted to make it known that he had no respect for anyone in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. I move to strike. It's one thing if he wants to introduce the statement, which again we've never had any discovery of. However, with regard to Lugar's mental thoughts, what if any mental thoughts Lugar had, I move to strike those, because this -- this witness cannot answer as to the intentions of Lugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He can only -- he can only tell us what happened or what he heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Simic, other than these verbal remarks -- no, rather, tell me, when did you first learn about the presence of the volunteers in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, because as the war went on, it became a publicly-known fact. But it was probably a few days after the breakout of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, in addition to these details, these verbal insults, do you have any other examples that would illustrate their attitude -- the attitude of Lugar and the others?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you any other examples because I did not have an opportunity to see them directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about their conduct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard all kinds of stories regarding some of them. I heard that they had been aggressive and so on, that they harassed the residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know which unit, which military formation they belonged to? Were they also members of this special battalion? If you know, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what their military association was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit P75, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this document, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this was one of the documents that had been sent at the time to various addresses in order to get assistance for the municipality that was in war.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Djordjevic is mentioned in this memo. Who is this man? His nickname is Vranjanac. Could you tell us who this man is.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when this memo was drafted, did you have any other details about Dragan Djordjevic? Did you know what his conduct was, what steps he had taken, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just knew that he was one of the volunteers and that he was some kind of a commander and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could we have now Exhibit P76.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us a brief comment on this document, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this document. I suppose that this document was prepared by the executive council and that later on it was prepared by the professional staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness said he didn't know the document, and then he's saying, I suppose that it was prepared -- so he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will clarify that. Maybe he doesn't know exactly this document, but maybe he's aware of the events or contents of this document or basis for issuance of this document. So that was my attempt to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, did you hear something about the content of this document? If you don't know, then just tell us so, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please could we have Exhibit P77.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, what do you know about this document? Was this document signed?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this document, and I see that there's no signature here, so I suppose that it was drafted in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. Once again, he doesn't know the document, and now he's trying to assume what happened to it. If he doesn't know, it's not a matter for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But -- well, his assumption also -- I mean, he's an educated man. He can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. Either a witness knows about something or he doesn't. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have -- sorry, could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me make it clear to you, Mr. Simic. You are a fact witness and you have come to the Tribunal to give evidence on matters which you know [Realtime transcript read in error "you don't know"]. If you don't know anything you say so, if you are shown a document you don't know it, you don't know have to assume anything. We don't want assumptions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P78, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at this document. But prior to that, let me ask you this: Are you familiar with the term "SAO Northern Bosnia"? Have you ever heard of it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a territorial administrative unit which was joined by the Samac municipality as well. The Crisis Staff did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you familiar with the SAO Semberija and Majevica?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I am familiar with the SAO Semberija and Majevica, not with the -- the other one. What did you say it was called, the first one? Could you please rephrase your question, because I have an impression that I mixed this up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem at all. I'm just waiting for the transcript. I want to make sure that everything is recorded here. I asked you whether you were familiar with the term "SAO Northern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not familiar with the SAO Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. My interjection -- I notice from the transcript that it said -- that referring to the witness, "You came to the Tribunal to give evidence on matters you don't know." I actually said, "You came to the Tribunal to give evidence on matters you know about."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Just for a clarification, yes, Your Honour. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you have heard about the SAO Semberija and Majevica. That's what you told us. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I have heard about it, but from what I remember, the Crisis Staff adopted a decision for the Samac municipality to join the SAO Semberija and Majevica. That is my response to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know something about the regulations and certain duties of the Crisis Staff, or rather, Samac municipality with respect to the SAO Semberija and Majevica?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a form of harmonisation of regulations, but that was within the jurisdiction of the executive council. I don't think that we ever adopted any decisions at the Crisis Staff sessions regarding this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please take a look at this decision in front of you. Tell us whether you have seen it before, whether you know something about it. If you don't, then just please tell us so.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this decision before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. You can get this document. Could we have, please, document P -- Exhibit P81, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this document, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Crisis Staff ever issued any orders to Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have please now Exhibit P82.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at this document. I think it has two pages. Can you tell us something about it. But please take a good look at it first.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are now in open session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could we have now Exhibit P83, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recognise this document, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have your comments to it, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision is related to the appointment of the commission for the exchange of detained and other persons, or rather, captured persons. And Mr. Maslic, Simo Nikolic, and Mr. Miroslav Tadic were members. And they were in charge of the exchange itself, prisoner exchange and the exchange of others. From what I can remember from talking to the president, they conducted the exchange of persons and for soldiers who had been captured. They would have to receive the okay from the military structures. As for people who had been detained by the police, those detainees -- and other people who were detained, they would have to receive permission from the police. For other citizens, I'm not sure of the details but I can give you an example based on my own personal experience. My wife had parents in Croatia. Her parents were in Croatia. And we asked Mr. Maslic together how we could get them out of Croatia, because information had reached us that they wished to leave Croatia and live with us. And he told us that the procedure was as follows: That he would first of all have to talk to the Croatian side. Then the Croatian side would have to ask the individuals, that is to say, her parents whether they wanted to leave, whether they wanted to go and live elsewhere of their own free will, and if they agreed, if they said yes, then the exchange would take place. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we could clarify. He said, "talking to the president." So could we ask the witness to specify which president. This is on page 30, line 12 onwards. About the commission he said, "From what I can remember from talking to the president," when talking of prisoner exchange. So could he specify which president, what he meant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, you said "I can remember from talking to the president." And then you went on to say that they conducted the exchange of persons and soldiers. So which president were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic. And in the document he is recorded as being the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we're on this topic, this is a document of the War Presidency dated the 2nd of October, 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as a member of the Crisis Staff yourself, did you happen to know in the period between April 1992 -- well, from April 1992 onwards, tell us what you know about the procedure for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I knew was that there was a commission in charge of these exchanges and that the exchanges were conducted in the following manner: For soldiers, permission had to be obtained from the military organs. For civilian detainees, it was the police, the police organs who had to grant permission. And if there were exchanges of citizens, then this would follow the procedure I described a moment ago, which means that the person to be exchanged would have to be asked if a citizen insisted on coming to the territory of Republika Srpska or in leaving that territory, the person would have to be asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a municipal commission. Do you know of any other commissions at different levels which dealt with exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did the Crisis Staff give its permission for individuals to be exchanged? Was it included in that process directly? Explain the role of the Crisis Staff, if it had a role to play within the subject of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff didn't deal in exchanges except for nominating and appointing the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the commission and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission's president would come to inform the Crisis Staff from time to time how things were going. They would look at some general principles and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Could we have Exhibit P85, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, tell us, please, whether you recognise this decision.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of the clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have it on the ELMO. Your Honour, maybe we could deal with this exhibit after the break, if that's an appropriate time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break and continue at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit P85.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, Mr. Simic, we were discussing this document, and you said that you have some personal knowledge about the circumstances which led up to the drafting of this document and some other important details.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is the following: At the time some civilians from the Odzak municipality, civilians who were Serbs, arrived on the territory of the Samac municipality. And it was necessary to ensure accommodation for them. And this decision shows the manner in which this was done. So those Serb citizens were to report to Kruskovo Polje, where accommodation for them would be organised. This was no easy task because in Samac municipality there were a large number of displaced persons there already, refugees, people who had lost their homes and who had to be put up somewhere, to find a safe haven for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said civilians of Serb ethnicity who had come into the Samac municipality territory. So these people, Serbs from Odzak, what status did they have and how did they come?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exchanged. That was the procedure. They were exchanged and they came into the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit P86, please -- no, no. Actually, no, I do apologise. That's just an exhibit regarding the appointment, so it is not directly related to -- I will try to speed up things. P88, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us anything about this document, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document doesn't come from the Crisis Staff, and I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain this for us, if there is the designation "the Crisis Staff of the municipality" and the seal there, how come you have concluded that this document doesn't come from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've concluded that based on the fact that this was done on a computer-type printer, so the text was created on computer and then printed on the printer. And from what I know, there were no such printers in the professional staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this topic? Was it discussed at the Crisis Staff? There are some looting cases mentioned here and so on.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these topics because these topics were associated with the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we have now Exhibit P90. 90, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recognise this document? What can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff ever issue any kind of permits to civilians in Samac municipality in order for them to be able to move freely about and leave the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff would occasionally issue a permit saying that such and such individual could leave the town and move about with that permit, and there would usually be a seal of the Crisis Staff on that permit. And as those people -- how did these people pass through checkpoints where permits were checked? I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please take a look at Article 2 and tell us whether there were any cases of this nature taking place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that permits were issued in the public security stations an in relevant military agencies, rather than in any civilian organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please clarify something that you've just told us. In which cases did the Crisis Staff issue permits?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain this for you. For example, if a member of the Crisis Staff or perhaps somebody who was part of some other service agency, if that person wanted to go elsewhere, therefore leave the territory of the municipality, then that person would be issued such a permit. That would be sealed with the Crisis Staff seal and such individuals could travel with such permits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these permits issued for people who needed to move about on official business or for private purposes?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those permits were issued by the head of the professional staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that some kind of a travel order or something similar?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff issue permits to people who were not of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the Samac residents who were non-Serbs? I mean, who was in charge of issuing permits to such residents?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have, please, Exhibit P91.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document looks familiar to me. The Crisis Staff passed this decision, namely to freeze the work of political organisations and political parties in order to prevent political conflicts which were undesirable at the time. However, this Article 2 deals with arrests. I know that this topic was not discussed, and I don't know how this issue got into this decision. I think that this was awkwardly done by the professional staff when they drafted the document. The Crisis Staff did not have any mechanism of the enforcing nature that would be able to do something like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell me this: At that time in the territory of Republika Srpska and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there any activity of political parties taking place?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have now Exhibit P92, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will remind you and tell you that the previous document was dated 12th of June, 1992. And now we can see the date 28th of November, 1992. This document was issued by the War Presidency. Can you comment to this decision.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When I said that the previous decision practically froze the activities of political parties, that didn't mean that any activity of theirs was banned by that order. That means that the parties could have a certain activity within their party bodies, and that is regulated by this decision that is in front of me now, which says that the parties could develop their own infrastructures and so on. And as far as I can remember, this decision had to do with that type of activity; namely, the Serb Democratic Party had to renovate and repair the old destroyed building of the hotel, and the party was supposed to prevent further decay of that building, and that was the purpose for passing this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this decision in fact transfer the ownership of the old hotel building to the SDS, or did this decision deal with something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was done later on by another decision of the assembly. This decision did not delve into that. It simply awarded temporary use of certain premises. It did not go into ownership issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the building of the old hotel was owned by whom at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was socially owned. At the time it was socially owned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Socially owned or state owned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because it is very difficult to translate that term into English. That category does not exist elsewhere. So could you please tell us what would be the closest term to the concept of social property.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have, please, now Exhibit P93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you comment on this decision dated 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This decision was adopted in order to try and prevent disorder in the town that was caused by various cafes and catering facilities that served liquor. At the time there was a lot of disorder, a lot of shooting, wounding incidents, and it was believed that one of the reasons for that was the fact that alcohol was served.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, now Exhibit P94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not an important document; however, it caused some debate and some questions in the past, so I would like to ask you to comment on this document. Do you perhaps remember this decision? And if so, can you tell us what was its objective, this decision or this certificate

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of a certificate could have been issued by the professional staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you just tell us, what is your interpretation of this certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a simple cut-and-dry certificate. What's he going to interpret or explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe it's just a question of language. Maybe he can say what he knows about it. But not in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Simple as that. Because we heard certain interpretations in previous proceedings which is completely contrary to the -- I mean, not in Defence case but, rather, in the Prosecution case. So I'm obliged to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead and explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this man wanted to transport his household goods from his parents' house to his own house. And in order to do so, he needed a certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the persons mentioned in the certificate?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of these persons mentioned here are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, now Exhibit P95, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us any comments regarding this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this decision because the Crisis Staff did not have its own treasury where funds could be kept. I presume this was something that had been done in the executive council. This is a nonsense, or at least the first article is, where it says, "Delivered to the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Samac."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, now Exhibit P96.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this meantime, let me ask you this: Did the Crisis Staff of Samac Municipality on any occasion engage persons to send weapons or people to the municipality? Did it have commissioners in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was never involved in those kinds of affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document and tell us what it represents, or rather, tell us whether you are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, again, is one of the documents that could have been issued by somebody from the professional staff to those people who were willing to assist with fund-raising, procuring of medications, and so on. However, I do not exclude the possibility that there could have been some abuses of these types of documents and that somebody could have used this document to collect money and funds elsewhere in the world for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 2 of this authorisation. It mentions trained people, sending of weapons and so on. Was there any talk of such activities?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff was never involved in such activities, nor did it have organs and services that dealt with such issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please could we have now Exhibit P98.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, please go ahead. Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the heading or the introductory part, one can conclude that this is a letter. Therefore, a written form of communication. At the time the Crisis Staff contacted different entities which it believed would be able to assist the imprisoned Serbs in the territory of Odzak municipality; therefore in Donja Dubica, Crnjak, Struke, Lipik, and Novi Grad. And there were between three and a half thousand and four thousand of them there. One of the letters, this one, to the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding these events in Odzak municipality in April and May of 1992, what did the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality do regarding this? What activities did you and other members of the Crisis Staff undertake regarding this in addition to writing letters?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to sending letters, appeals, and other ways of engaging the public, the Crisis Staff tried to engage the public in Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I really meant the practical steps. What practical steps were taken? What contacts did they establish with the other side, and so on? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time a coordination body was established comprising of people that would be able to establish contact with the? People over there and try and get some assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you give us any details what was done? You were in the field of information, so you should be able to give us more details regarding this. We are interested in that period of time it's very important to us.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just told you, those people, some 3500 to 4.000 of them were in prison there, and many of them had relatives in Samac municipality and in other places, and these relatives tried to help the imprisoned people. It was difficult to do, and it was a very difficult process. That agony lasted all the way up until the first exchanges started, and they were quite a relief to the population. All of these appeals and letters that were sent, everything that was done by the Crisis Staff and other organs of civilian authorities, the Red Cross and so on, none of it was fruitful for a long period of time, and it was only later that they managed to ensure that people started arriving into Samac municipality, naturally very happy that they were able to leave and unite with their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me who made up this coordinating body.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we decided to do it this way, and we thought that was the best way of doing it: For us to ensure contact with the people, that body should be made up, we thought, of people from -- from local people who knew the situation, who knew the families, who knew the individuals, and who would be able to compile a list of persons who found themselves there. And that is why the members were Mr. Miroslav Tadic, Mr. Simo Zaric, and Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who were from the area. Mr. Tadic was born in Novi Grad. For example, Mr. Simo Zaric was born in Crnjak. And Mr. Bozo Ninkovic was a native of Donja Dubica, that village, the village in the Odzak municipality. And then they continued these activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Crisis Staff involved in contacts with any internal organisations perhaps at that period of time? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that at one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff a report was presented to show that people from the International Red Cross had engaged in that activity, that they cooperated with the people from the coordinating body and that in that sense they had some joint solutions. And they organised, I think, a joint exchange programme and the exchange took place - took place, yes, that's a better word - on the Bosna River. It is a river which separates the municipalities of Odzak and Samac. I think in that first exchange in which the International Red Cross participated, about 100 persons were exchanged, Serb civilians, and people captured on the Odzak municipality territory. And we all remember that because it was something that reverberated and was publicly known. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was done at a municipal level with respect to resolving humanitarian issues, problems of accommodation for those people, in the month of May, if I'm right?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the civilian protection or civil defence headquarters had been set up and was functioning, and they saw to the accommodation of refugees and displaced persons who had been exchanged in the -- from the Odzak municipality and other areas as well, and this service had a heavy burden to bear. They had a very difficult job to do because there was an influx of people coming into the territory of Samac municipality and they had been left without their houses. They had left their property behind. They had no means of livelihood. They were usually separated from their families. And sometimes these people were just not able to find their way and live a normal life because it was difficult to ensure food supplies and everything that was needed for a normal life. And this was one of the most serious problems and difficult periods that we faced, because there were many, many people coming into the Samac municipality who were left without the basic means of livelihood and survival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Solving these humanitarian problems for the Serb refugees from the Odzak municipality when they arrived in Samac, did this jeopardise and threaten certain rights of the non-Serb inhabitants in Samac in any way?
