Could you explain to us how this was done. Were the non-Serbs evicted, for example, from their homes for these Serbs to take up accommodation there? Did they take over their flats, or what happened? What did you do in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any more detailed information about this because the service for accommodation within the municipality was in charge of this matter. But as far as I know, there were no human rights violations. Human rights were not curtailed and the members of other ethnic groups were not in jeopardy at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we're on the subject, were you a witness -- or rather, did you see that the non-Serb population in Samac in 1992/1993, did you see them wearing white bands on their sleeves when they moved around town perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: White bands you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any white bands or ribbons. Nobody had any white bands. But I can say that this was a sort of propaganda ploy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a journalist, Mr. Mato Krajinovic was his name, launched a piece of information along those lines over the radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, sometime in June. And I am deeply convinced that this was imported, this information, and that the source was his propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a criticism to make of the translation. When he mentioned accommodation for the refugees, and it is line 44, page 21, he said, "I don't know anything much about that because the Secretariat for Communal Matters." Where it says "accommodation service" here, perhaps we could clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you said that the communal services or the secretariat was in charge of this, what were you thinking about?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The housing and communal department in the municipality. That's what I had in mind. And I assume that it was that department who was in charge of seeing to affairs of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's get back to our white bands or ribbons. Did you or the Crisis Staff or some third party ever issue orders to Radio Samac to broadcast the order for non-Serbs to wear these white bands or ribbons?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff never made any such decision, nor did it issue orders to Radio Samac to broadcast anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were linked to the information department, do you perhaps know whether any third party issued orders to the radio to broadcast this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No service or organ of any kind, as far as I know, issued any such orders or gave any such instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you know, did Radio Samac broadcast an order by the Public Security Station on banning any rallies of persons -- more than three persons in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Radio Samac never broadcast anybody's orders, and it never broadcast any information or news of that kind at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have, please, Exhibit 100 -- P100. Excuse me, my mistake. P99.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already spoken about a series of letters. We're not going to make any more comments because I think you've explained it sufficiently. But tell me, is this -- are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document along the lines of the letters and appeals through which you addressed the public and international agencies?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have P100 [Realtime transcript read in error "P10"], please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked about this subject. What can you tell me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Could we have P100. Because in transcript it's only P10, so just for clarification of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Samac municipality pursuant to this decision, Semberija and Majevica -- or rather, this decision was for practical reasons. Samac was completely surrounded. It was encircled, and there was no way in which it could have been linked into a territorial hole with the municipalities of Odzak, Orasje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "surrounded," "encircled"?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Samac municipality is located -- it looks like a wedge and comes out onto the River Sava. And through the River Sava -- across the river is the Republic of Croatia. And on the two flanks are the municipalities of Odzak and Orasje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a geographical explanation, but let's be more practical, Mr. Simic. We're talking about May 1992. And I'm interested to know who surrounded the Samac municipality. Give us some names, institutions, or whatever. Not geography. We don't want geography at this point.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the River Sava was the Croatian army, and almost every day - because there was nobody else who could have shelled the area - it was the Croatian army that shelled the town on a daily basis, the town and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, move south and tell us what other forces were -- what was around Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Odzak municipality, the HVO, the Croatian HVO, the Croatian -- I can't remember what the HVO stood for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That's right. That's it, the Croatian Defence Council. Members of the HVO were in Orasje as well, the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Orasje in relation to Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: East, to the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: North, south, east, or west?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: East.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was to the south?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the south was the municipality of Gradacac, which is where the allied forces of the HVO and Muslims launched their operations, armed forces. And I have to say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was Samac under siege for?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samac was completely under siege, completely encircled --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just asking for how long. Up until what date?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade made this military break-through and the municipality of Samac was linked as a result to the Krajina municipalities from the Banja Luka region to the west, and on the east with Semberija and Majevica. And that was the corridor that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P101, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we're going to take a look at this next document, which is linked to SAO Majevica. In May 1992 before the corridor, what was the reason for the municipality to be linked up with this corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons were practical reasons. They were to link up the administration and the various institutions and to form one whole, one entity. They were not able to exist separately. They had to be linked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But hierarchically speaking, if we look at hierarchy, we know that the Bosanski Samac municipality was at one level. What was the next level up? Could you explain the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next step up the ladder was the SAO. This was a kind of canton. And then we come to the state level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the municipal organs, were the decisions of SAO Semberija and Majevica binding upon them?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not binding upon the municipal orders of the SAO Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the republican organs?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were. They were binding, which means that this was some sort of shaky system. For example, if there was a patient who needed medical attention in Samac and had to be treated in Bijeljina, we had a practical problem if we didn't have an administrative solution to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, about this decision: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am particularly interested in Article 2. Can you comment on it, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't really see this article practically implemented either by the Crisis Staff or in the municipality itself. I think it was put in there for some formal reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the voting procedure of the Crisis Staff, I suppose, was such that everybody had -- every member had one vote. Is that right, or was there different voting procedure?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've already explained that. Since the president of the Crisis Staff wanted to include always a large number of people in the debate and in the decision-making, then very often there was no voting taking place at all. Positions were harmonised and then a sort of consensus was reached, although sometimes we did vote on issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any cases where, for example, a proposal by Blagoje Simic was outvoted in voting procedure, or did he have some kind of an authority?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If his proposal was outvoted, he had to uphold the results of the vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any cases where his proposals were outvoted?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a specific example, but I suppose that there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of that, you were an assemblyman in the assembly and you know a lot about parliament and parliamentary issues. What is the role of the president of the assembly? What are his duties, and what is his real power?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I was an assemblyman in the assembly. I was not a deputy in the state parliament. And I will answer your question. You would like to know what are the authorities of the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To convene sessions of the municipal assembly; to propose agendas; to ensure that items are debated; to ensure that after a decision is passed, the decision is handed over to the professional staff for them to complete their task and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the president's vote stronger than a vote of any other assemblyman?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And as to the weight of that vote, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Exhibit P102, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues wanted me to clarify something. When you spoke about the weight of the president's vote, what were you trying to say. If an issue was voted on, then what did your answer relate to?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this comment of mine was probably unnecessary under the circumstances. What I was trying to say was that each vote was just a single vote. And even if the president was outvoted, the will of the majority was upheld. And my comment was meant to convey that if somebody had an authority, not necessarily president of the assembly but somebody else, then it might have influenced the outcome of the vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's be more specific. What authority does president of the have?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authority of the municipal assembly is quite limited because the municipality deals with the utilities and the infrastructure, with things that have to do with the everyday life of the residents. It does not deal with different issues. And in that respect, its influence is quite limited. I hope that this is what you wanted me to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, could you make a comparison between the president of the executive council and this president. How can you -- what kind of a correlation can you make there? How can you describe this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can describe it in the following terms --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question did not relate to the correlation. I wanted you to make a comparison.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where we come from - and I think this applies to other places as well - the executive branch has more authority for a simple reason, that it has at its disposal financial means and other types of power, so that the executive branch was always much more powerful, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you the following: This document was prepared by the executive council. And as such, it was ratified by the Crisis Staff. I really couldn't tell you anything about the items mentioned in this document because this is something that had been done by the executive council, by the people who are professionals in that particular field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But based on what you know, were there any cases of confiscation or seizure of property of some individuals due to tax evasion by those individuals?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such cases where property was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have now Exhibit P105, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another document. On page 3 we can see that it is dated 15th of December, 1992. Do you know anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I've never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, now Exhibit P106.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us something about this document, if you know, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision is familiar to me. It was passed at the time when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put it on the ELMO so that our clients can see the document as well. And then if you don't mind, you can also look at it there.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision abolished Crisis Staffs in local communes and instead of them appointed commissioners; namely, at that time it was believed that a large number of people was in the Crisis Staffs in local communes when there was a large need for personnel in the military and there was a work obligation in existence. And as a result of that, these Crisis Staffs were abolished because they were at the level of local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the objective of those Crisis Staffs in local communes?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as in municipalities. They were meant to act in extraordinary circumstances, to help after the shelling and wounding of the population, to ensure that life went on in local communes, to house refugees, to assist people with health problems, and so on. Samac at the time faced a lot of difficult problematic situations. There were about 50 patients with a kidney condition who needed to undergo haemodialysis twice a week. And as a result of that, it was difficult to transport them, to secure fuel for that, to find dialysis machines, and so on. I don't want to go into the strictly professional part of this matter, but I know that people who had to undergo dialysis three times a week were only able to do it twice a week because there was an insufficient number of dialysis machines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the ethnicity of those patients.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of them were Serbs, but there was also Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, regarding the Crisis Staffs in local communes, can you tell us what other elements constituted a municipality.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A municipality had an executive council --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. Let's take a look at the territory of a municipality. Can you tell us what does a municipality consist of in a territorial sense. What are lower-level units of it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were local communes -- actually, every village was a local commune, and Samac municipality had 20 such local communes with some 30.000 residents. The town itself had 5.000 residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Exhibit P [Previous interpretation continues] ... Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. P107.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It wasn't reflected on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to spend too much time on this document, but tell me whether you're familiar with it and what was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to appoint individuals who would perform this function of commissioner and that they should report back and be responsible to the Crisis Staff and the executive board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that this followed on from when the system was simplified, and you explained the reasons for the abolishment of the other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- P108, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me something about this document.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am aware of the decision. It's familiar to me. But I'm not familiar with the preamble. This decision was made so that the town of Bosanski Samac should be referred to and the name of the town be just Samac. And the explanation given was that there is a town called Slavonski Samac and there was the Croatian municipality of Bosanski Samac, so the reason why this decision was taken was to make the distinction between these, to differentiate between this and the others. And they thought why not give the town the name of Samac, just Samac, because it was very difficult to find anybody who actually called it Bosanski Samac. Everybody would just simply say Samac for the name of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the municipality -- the Croatian municipality, the opstina of Bosanski Samac. Was that a separate municipality or was it something else? Could you explain what you mean.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bosanski Samac -- this Bosanski Samac was formed by the Croats in the part of the territory of Samac municipality which was not under the control of the Serb forces but the Croatian forces, and it incorporated several villages, Domaljevac, Grebnice, Prud, Bazik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb forces ever occupy that part of the municipality which was inhabited by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The Croatian authorities were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, population-wise, inhabitant-wise, let's say from March 1992. Not April. I'm saying March specifically. Let's take the month of March 1992 and then right up to the present day. The inhabitants on the territory of Croatian Bosanski Samac, are those people still there? Are they still living there? Or were they on Serb territory at one point? Could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizens who were of Croatian ethnicity in the municipality or villages of Domaljevac, Grebnice, Bazik, Prud, which means the villages which at one time belonged to the municipality of Bosanski Samac, continued to -- that is to say, the population continued to live there and they had their own administrative units, and it was the Croatian municipality of Bosanski Samac, and the headquarters were in Domaljevac. So that is one of the municipalities within the Orasje canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom does the Orasje canton belong?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belongs to the BH Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is BH and the BH Federation?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the entities of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- P109, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this document, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document speaks of the appointment of the president of the Crisis Staff. He was appointed on the 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the date is the 17th of April on that document.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already explained that, that it was for purposes of the work booklets and linking up the work periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have document P110 and 111, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, please, Mr. Simic. Let's not waste too much time on these less-important documents. Tell me, please, do you know anything about these two documents? Look at both of them, please. I can see that the decision was made by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend this Crisis Staff meeting. I wasn't there on that particular day. But I do know that after the meeting the president of the Crisis Staff, Blagoje Simic, was very unhappy. He didn't like the outcome, the election -- the choice of president or vice-president of the executive council. And as I learnt, his candidate was Mr. Mirko Lukic. I, too, considered that -- I shared his opinion. I thought that that would be a better option because of nepotism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is why the president of the Crisis Staff didn't think it was a good idea to have people with the same surnames holding high-level positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He says "I think." Is he speculating, or is that a comment that he received directly from Blagoje Simic? If it's a comment from discussions with Blagoje Simic, I have no problem with that and I withdraw the objection. But if it's just his speculation, I think it should be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have, please, Exhibit P112.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us something about this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was prepared by the executive council and I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember that it was discussed and then adopted at the Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just can't seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P113, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, a document.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an authorisation signed by Mr. Mitar Mitrovic, who was the secretary, and it relates to the granting of authorisation to Mr. Stevan Todorovic -- or it authorises Stevan Todorovic to represent the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac at an assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which would be held beginning with the 25th of July, 1992 until the end of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but we're dealing with the War Presidency here, are we? And you were a member of it, were you?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing, please: This authorisation in this form, was it discussed at the meeting of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just what I was about to say. This authorisation was signed by Mr. Mitar Mitrovic, which means that he wrote it too. And the explanation he gives is that Mr. Todorovic insisted and tried to convince him and kept pestering him to let him go there, and he said he was not going to attend the assembly but just going there for a little bit. Mr. Todorovic liked to amuse himself, and so he wanted to take a trip but said he wouldn't actually be taking part in the work of the assembly, and in fact he couldn't have taken part in the work of the assembly. He could have just perhaps been there as an observer, in the capacity of an observer or some other capacity, but not as a participant. That wasn't his status. He couldn't take part as a deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he," do you mean Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I mean Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And what about Blagoje Simic? Was Blagoje Simic able to represent the municipal assembly at the popular assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not able to representative -- it either because Mr. Blagoje Simic likewise was not a deputy of the popular Assembly of Republika Srpska, and there was no grounds for him to participant except as a guest or observer or some such status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember and tell us -- or do you know whether anybody from the region of the Samac municipality was a member of parliament of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mirko Jovanovic was a member of the parliament of Republika Srpska, and he became a member of the People's Assembly or parliament after the death of a deputy by the name of Bjelosevic from Derventa. Mr. Jovanovic was next to him on the list, right after him on the list of the SDS party, and it was by that token that he became a deputy in the parliament of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I can't remember. But it was probably as soon as the first assembly was convened, because I do know that one of the deputies, Mr. Bjelosevic, was killed right at the beginning of the war. He was a colleague of mine. He was also a professor, a teacher of the Serbo-Croatian language, and I knew him personally, so that I know when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you be a bit more specific. Can you give us a month, a year? Give me the year. You said the beginning of the war, but it's not specific enough.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, please, the reason stated here, the reason given -- or rather, this authorisation makes mention of the fact that Blagoje Simic was undergoing hospital treatment. In the period after July, did he attend the meetings of the War Presidency, and how frequent were the meetings? How often were they held?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the time he didn't come. He didn't attend the sessions for a long time of period. At that time, the sessions of the Crisis Staff were infrequent, and if a document needed to be issued or something like that, then that was carried out by the professional staff. So the work of the Crisis Staff was -- how shall I put it? -- not very active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to make a tiny correction. You are speaking of the Crisis Staff, are you? That's a bit confusing to me, because we see the date of the 25th of July and I am asking you about the time from that date onwards. What did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the War Presidency, of course. However, ten years have passed and my memory is not as fresh as it used to be, so sometimes it's difficult for me to distinguish between these two terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have another question before the break, but if you're tired, just let us know and we can make a break at any time. When you compare the sessions of the Crisis Staff from April 1992 to July of 1992 with the sessions of the War Presidency from July of 1992 until the end of that year, what kind of a conclusion can you make?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the work of the Crisis Staff was much more dynamic and active than that of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that. Do you mean in terms of the number of sessions or what?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of sessions, the scope of issues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the situation was such. When the War Presidency was established, the situation had become more normal and more reasonable. The life was already better organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which organs became more involved?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular organs. New institutions were formed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's be more specific. Which organs at the level of Samac municipality started taking over work?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started preparing the session of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, which was held in January 1993 for the first time. However, the executive council was working in full composition, as were other institutions, and in one word the life became more normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me which segments comprised the executive council? Can you tell us which organs were in it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had several departments that -- in addition to the president of the executive council, we had Secretary for Economy, Secretary for Housing and Utilities, Secretary for Education and Culture, Secretary for General Administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's maybe an appropriate time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 18.05 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We just received -- I mean, this afternoon, prior to the session, the Prosecution response to our motion in respect to Rule 71. And if the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that maybe the Defence could in five minutes maybe today give certain clarifications. It's not a classical reply, but maybe it would be helpful for the Trial Chamber in order to rule on this issue of Rule 71. It might be useful. I mean, with your permission to -- if we can address the Trial Chamber on several matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. How long do you think you have to go with the witness? When are you finishing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I have to comment with him around 20 documents and some other issues and events. I believe that I would finish him next sitting day very shortly. It will be far less than -- provided that -- than the estimated time. I was of the opinion that it was -- it would be 10 hours. But it will be less than 10 hours, so I am -- in terms of the consumption of time, I think it would be -- it would be a certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So maybe you'll go ahead with the witness and then the last 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The last 10 minutes maybe would be fine, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, before the break, we touched upon several topics. You gave us your answers. Now, tell me, please, did the War Presidency sometime in the fall of 1992 send a letter to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia regarding the repeated arrival of volunteers from Serbia to the Samac municipality? Was this discussed at the sessions of the War Presidency and what do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency was never involved in the issues of military organisations and military issues in general, so nothing of that nature was ever discussed at the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the activities of the Crisis Staff from May to June 1992 regarding the appointment -- nomination and appointment of the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that anybody in the Crisis Staff was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it discussed at the sessions of the Crisis Staff perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please, what do you know about the incident linked to the closing of the corridor in the autumn of 1992, from October to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very little about that event. The only thing that I do know is that there was some kind of a conflict between military and civilian authorities and that the closing of the corridor was the result of that conflict. Now, as to details, I don't know anything regarding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But do you know who closed off the corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the conflict between military and civilian authorities that you have mentioned? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that throughout the war that conflict continuously went on, the conflict between the military and civilian authorities. I know that in September of 1993 that conflict culminated in Banja Luka and resulted in the situation in which the military authorities took over the entire town. Karadzic and Mladic had a conflict between them. One was the representative of the civilian authorities, and the other represented military authorities, and this issue was covered in the media as well. These two components clashed in wartime, and there was some kind of a tension between civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned Banja Luka and 1993, and I assume that's --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1993. This is a well-known event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But that was at a higher level, at the level of the republic and level of high authorities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That was not our topic. I am interested in the municipal level at the end of 1992. You mentioned that there was a conflict there as well. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were certain --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a letter mentioned. I did not have occasion to read the letter. It was sent by the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade and in it the army criticised the civilian authorities. However, I couldn't go into details of that letter because I didn't have occasion to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know about the arrest of Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that very period they were arrested. I don't know the reasons for their arrest, but it had to do with the conflict between military and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that problem finally resolved, and what was the outcome, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was the outcome or what was the way in which it was resolved. I don't know what was behind it either. I don't know what it was all about. I have no information regarding that. I know that after that there followed arrests of certain volunteers from the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade and that they were, I suppose, in the military investigative prison in Banja Luka. Now, as to the results of that investigation, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In autumn of 1992, were these volunteers present in the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. After their arrest, they did not come back to Samac municipality. I don't know what was their fate afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have just a second, please, to check documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have Exhibit D46/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please comment on this decision.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have D45/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us something about this document? Are you familiar with it? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this discussed at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit D55/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a payroll or salary list for 1992, March [As interpreted]. Does it reflect the actual state of affairs as regards the members of the Crisis Staff and their salaries?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The month is May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript. It's a payroll list for May 1992. Because on page 68, line 3, it said "March 1992." So just for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list does reflect the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have D63/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at page 2 of the document, please. But before you do, tell me what you can tell us in general about this.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this article was published in the Samac Koridor newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a newspaper? What is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, actually, it's a magazine which was published in Samac from the end of 1992 until 1998. And this is one of the articles published in Koridor, the periodical. The author of the article is Vaso Antic, a journalist, and he wanted to show what the situation was like at that time when dialysis functioned -- or rather, when the patients who needed dialysis as a treatment had problems, encountered problems, because the Samac municipality had a lot of problems with the dialysis machines and everything linked to haemodialysis. And they managed through the International Community and some institutions to ensure the resources they needed and the technical equipment they needed. However, despite all that, the situation was still very difficult. The centre for haemodialysis, which you can see on the photograph here, was targeted persistently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at page 2 of the article, please, and see whether among the patient statements you can tell us which person belonged to which ethnic group, if you're able to say that.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Stevo Vukovic, from Crkvina, was a Serb. Todo Babic [phoen], from Donja Slatina, was a Serb lady. Jozo Stevanovic was from Crkvina, a Serb again. Munira Ziamovic, a lady from Samac was a Muslim. Ferida Islamovic [phoen], also from Samac was a Muslim lady. Danica Pacak also from Samac. I can't tell you what she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read her statement. Take a look at what she says.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She says that she's been going to dialysis treatment for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm interested in her ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's a Croat lady.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when was this periodical founded?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The periodical named Koridor was founded at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- D58/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us something about this document perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is one of the documents which relate to certain appointments for individuals and cadres, coordinators of certain companies, institutions, et cetera. And Mr. Mesud Nogic was appointed to the post of coordinator in the health centre of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether you know how long he continued in that post.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Nogic performed this duty right up until the time that he decided to leave Samac as his place of residence. And I think he went abroad, but I'm not quite sure. I don't know where he went, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give me a date?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ethnicity was Dr. Nogic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Nogic was a Muslim, or rather, he was a Bosniak, of Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have, please, Exhibit D64/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me what you can say about the document. The period of time is November 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when the public civil engineering enterprise was set up, and it included the bricklaying factory in Novi Grad and the delta of the Bosna River -- actually, these were two companies which merged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the object of this undertaking?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the town at that time had been largely destroyed, so the object of setting up a company of this kind was to build up the town, to repair the buildings that had been damaged, to do some civil engineering work where it was needed, and to build up the town again, rebuild it. That was the object for this company being set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know that in some enterprises in 1992 and 1993 - these are the years that we're interested in in this trial - that workers of all ethnic groups found employ?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got any complete information and data about that, but I do know for certain that in many companies there were workers who belonged to all the ethnic groups or the three main ethnic groups, because in Samac we have Croats, Serbs, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can take this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few more documents here which I can show you, but perhaps we could take them all together through my questions. The Crisis Staff, did it make decisions to authorise fodder, feed, animal feed for farmers who produced livestock? Do you remember the Crisis Staff discussing topics like that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the -- the Crisis Staff work that I took part in, we did not discuss topics of that kind, but I assume that when members of the executive council were present, they did discuss such issues. So with regard to animal feed and fodder --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I didn't actually -- tell me in principle. Do you happen to know whether the Crisis Staff or any other organs of the municipality in 1992 and 1993 made efforts to ensure that farming on the farms -- tell us a little about that, because you belonged to the information department. So quote a few examples. And it was 1992 and 1993. And what was done in this area?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a priority task to capacitate those resources which were linked to food production and so capacitate these farms and other facilities and resources. So these were priority tasks. That, I do know. Now, how this was done, what methods were used to promote food production, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I didn't mean you to go into those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit D60/3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this document, Mr. Simic? Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was taken to solve a practical problem. The members of the army, soldiers that were refugees from the refugee population, the problem was where to bury them. In Samac soldiers were buried who were from the local area, from those local communities and communes, and we had the problem of where to bury people who were originally refugees. And the cemeteries were full. There wasn't enough room to bury these people. So this decision was made to try and resolve the issue, to regulate matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know how many inhabitants were killed -- Samac inhabitants were killed during the war?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, around 90 -- between 80 and 90. You mean the municipality or the town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 80 and 90 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This figure applies to civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this figure apply to all three ethnic groups or ...?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number does apply to all three ethnic groups, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps happen to know -- it's difficult, I know, to go into the details, but generally speaking, how these people lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people, for the most part, were killed because they were hit by artillery projectiles. On rare occasions did people die from bullets. Usually they were artillery projectiles that they were hit by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many wounded civilians were there?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a far larger number. There were probably many more people who were injured and wounded. The figure must have been several times higher. And I saw some people being killed myself. If this august Tribunal would like to hear my experiences, what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Briefly, then.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the shelling in May, when several civilians died in a single day. I was on the ground then and I was present at one such situation -- or rather, I came shortly after the shelling. That happened in Crkvina in front of the house of Nikola Maslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Maslic, a peasant woman, was in front of her shelter wearing her clothes and a shrapnel went through her chest. That was an awful sight that I still have in my mind, one of horrible incidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since members of all three ethnic groups, civilians from all three ethnic groups were killed, can you tell us this: Did the non-Serbs have their own burial procedures? Was it all done regularly? Or did it only apply to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three cemeteries in Samac. One is an Orthodox one. The other one is a Catholic cemetery. And the third one is a Muslim one. Funerals were performed in cemeteries depending on the ethnic origin. That's how it was before the war, during the war, and today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were religious ceremonies observed for each ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Ms. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D58/3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you familiar with this decision of the War Presidency, dated November 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwriting is not very legible, but I think that this is a conclusion that has to do with the convening of the municipal assembly session, and I do remember that. So the session was being prepared, the one that was to be held on the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when that happened, did the War Presidency terminate its work, once the municipal assembly became operational?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Once the municipal assembly was convened, the War Presidency was abolished and the assembly started functioning together with all of its organs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Usher. Ms. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D59/3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was adopted in April of 1992. It was necessary then to ensure that the municipal staff of civilian protection was fully operational; therefore, Mr. Miroslav Tadic was appointed to this post. And upon being appointed to this post, he also became a member of the Crisis Staff, and his term within the Crisis Staff continued until the War Presidency was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the scope of activities of the civilian protection staff? What did they generally deal with?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff had many tasks because many houses were destroyed, a lot of buildings were ruined, many institutions could not operate on account of that, and a lot of work had to be done in order to make it all operational. This staff worked on these matters around the clock, and the people who worked there were very, very busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, please tell me, what do you know about providing food for the civilian population of Samac in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the situation was like: The supply of food into town from the villages was interrupted. There was also no supply of medication and any other goods. Therefore, the municipality had to rely on its internal reserves and to find some alternative methods of acquiring goods from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that initial period, were there any activities undertaken in order to feed the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the fact that there was no supply of food and goods, the civilian protection staff organised the feeding of the population by setting up certain food distribution sites. They distributed bread, cans, baby food, and even cigarettes occasionally, but it was mostly intended for the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the situation in the villages. What you just told us was about the town itself. And what was it like in the villages?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation in villages was better. People in villages had more food because they had their fields and their own production of bread and they had cattle and other types of food, and all of that was lacking in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. And what was the situation like in the village of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was the same as in other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it an appropriate time maybe to address the Trial Chamber with the issue with regard to the Rule 71?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom. The proceedings will continue on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. As I said, the Defence received a Prosecution response to the joint Defence motion made in respect of Rule 71. The Prosecution response was dated the 29th of November, this year. The Defence would like to -- to express its opinion in order to assist the Trial Chamber in the rendering of relevant decision. Just several remarks: In principle, we absolutely do not have any objections with regard to the issue of video testimony, videolink, so we are on the same line -- same track with the Prosecution with regard to this proposition. Of course, the final -- the final decision will be, of course, of the Trial Chamber. That's the first thing. The second thing, with the -- regard to the some -- some other things: In paragraph 12 of this response, the Prosecution mentioned several names of the witnesses for the defendant Mr. Blagoje Simic, and the names are Mitar Mitrovic, Savo Popovic, Slobodan Sjencic, Milan Pisarevic, and Momcilo Krajisnik. Just for the record, the Defence states that Mr. Slobodan Sjencic with a member of the executive board, not a member of the Crisis Staff. And Milan Pisarevic was just in pre-time -- pre-war period was just a secretary of SDS municipal branch. So neither Mr. Sjencic nor Mr. Pisarevic were members of the Crisis Staff. Just as a matter of clarity With regard to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, of course -- the Defence was not of the opinion that Mr. Krajisnik, in case that our request should be granted, should travel to Belgrade to give testimony in accordance with Rule 71. However -- I mean, our -- our understanding was if Mr. Krajisnik will give his testimony, that it will be in the premises of the Tribunal or by way of Rule 92 bis at the premises of UNDU. With regard to Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to reiterate that the Defence raised that issue with regard to Variant A and B during the proceedings in the Prosecution case. We got in mind several names, but in order to respect consumption of time of Defence case, we make our choice that Mr. Krajisnik will simply answer the question of his personal knowledge of Variant A and B. I have consent of his lawyer. I made the necessary contacts. And in terms of time, it will be not more than, let's say, five minutes. Because it's only one question. So there is not any -- any kind of big cross-examination or -- of course cross-examination could be limited only to the issue of that personal knowledge -- potential personal knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik with regard to the existence of so-called Variant A and B. So that is the -- Another thing which the Defence could like to reiterate: That we could of course -- we could of course make some variations with regard to the time, but the issue of a public hearing in terms of Rule 71, the Defence is of the opinion that it's a rather strange approach of the Prosecution, because the term of the position is not related to the principle of publicity. It's rather more flexible and more, I would say, practical way how the parties can in a process of searching of truth can -- can do their job in accordance with the common law standards. And then this documents -- I mean the transcripts or videotapes could be tendered in the evidence of the -- in the case by itself, and finally the Trial Chamber will make an evaluation of each of these exhibits. And our understanding of the spirit of Rule 71 is that in the interests of justice, in the interest of judicial economy and in accordance with the certain budgetary problems, the parties should give their personal attempt in order to respect all these three principles, and therefore Rule 71 was introduced. Otherwise, what would be the sense of Rule 71 in our proceedings? Thank you. That's from the part of Mr. Blagoje Simic's Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very brief, but I would like us to turn into private session due to some details regarding the witness that I have proposed. I would just like to say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the second argument advanced by the Prosecution, I don't see why they are objecting to the second witness for Miroslav Tadic, because they didn't say anything regarding that beforehand. I would also like to add that Defence of Miroslav Tadic tried to reduce even more the time envisaged for these depositions so that with respect to the time initially envisaged, we have now reduced it to less than one hour per witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in addition, Your Honour, if it may assist the Trial Chamber, if that's a problem, the Defence for Blagoje Simic can limit it -- can limit their witnesses in Rule 71 to the following -- to the following persons: Mr. Sjencic, then Mr. Duekovic, Colonel Vujinovic, and Mr. Krajisnik. So in total, from our list, we could have these four persons instead of seven, so in order to be complete. If they may assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. What you're saying -- these you have mentioned are the ones -- if the Trial Chamber were to cut down, you'd rather have these on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If there is a necessity to cut down the number of Defence witnesses, then we could be satisfied with these four names, because I think that we shall even make certain limitations in terms of time for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- these four. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not to repeat what my learned colleagues have already said, but we really, really do feel that it is in the interests of justice that these depositions be performed in any way that is provided for by the rules and regulations. We feel strongly on that score. In preparing this submission, we have given our proposals for nine depositions and we have reduced them to the smallest number possible to be taken. As things now stand - and we were guided by this - was that they were short statements to brief episodes, events, and I don't think that these depositions as far as the witnesses proposed are concerned, proposed by Mr. Zaric's Defence, will not be long ones. They were short meetings, short contacts, and we can also say that each of these depositions which we are proposing will not last longer than 20 minutes -- 25 to 30 minutes at the most. And also, if the Trial Chamber decides to reduce the number of depositions, we should like to ask that we, the Defence counsel, should be allowed to decide which witnesses we're going to select. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. The Trial Chamber will make its -- you wanted to reply, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just very briefly to several matters. Mr. Lukic seems to misunderstand the Prosecution's position. We are not objecting to his calling deposition -- his calling those witnesses. We are objecting only to a category of witnesses which we say is inappropriate to be called as deposition witnesses. And it's set out in our response, so I won't go into that. The other point I wish to make is in relation to Mr. Krajisnik. It's a very important point. My learned friend Mr. Pantelic says it will only take five minutes. Well, he may only be five minutes in his examination-in-chief of Mr. Krajisnik, but the Prosecution will be much, much, much longer, because there are many issues relating to the heart of this matter of this case which we will put to Mr. Krajisnik, as we will have to put our case to him as the president of the National Assembly at the time and the instructions given by the government to the local Crisis Staffs. He would take a long, long time; not five minutes. That's -- that's fairy tale stuff in my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber will take the decision as soon as possible so that the parties know which witnesses will go under Rule 71. Of course there may be -- there may be variations. And depending on how the Trial Chamber feels, some witnesses may be -- it may be important for the Trial Chamber to observe them so that they may have to come as viva voce witnesses. But the decision will be rendered as soon as possible. We shall adjourn and continue our proceedings on Tuesday. The times are as per the calendar.
